notes.plans: After capturing the bishop, Black should reposition the bishop to a safe square like d6, pressuring the knight on f4 and preparing to open the position.

notes.explains: With the bishop pair and White's bad piece on a2, Black wants to open the board. The move d4 is good because it temporarily sidelines White's bishop.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair and the opponent has a poorly placed piece, aim to open the position to increase your advantage.
notes.plans: Black can consider Queen B8, building a battery against the knight on f4, or Rook f8-e8 contesting the e-file. The tactic after Knight takes d5 is Bishop takes g3 forking queen and knight.

notes.explains: Queen B8 is a strong move because it threatens to take on f4 twice and prevents Knight takes d5 due to the fork on g3. It also keeps the e7 square defended by the knight, stopping checks.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that create multiple threats and improve your piece coordination, especially when the opponent's pieces are tied down.
notes.plans: After Queen B8, White's best defenses are Queen d2 or Knight e5. Black should be ready to handle either, but Queen d2 is less dangerous.

notes.explains: The queen on d2 is a safe square that allows the bishop to go to e4, where it is secure and pressures weak squares in White's territory.
notes.teaches: When a queen move defends a key square and also enables a powerful piece placement, it can be a strong defensive and offensive idea.
notes.plans: Play Bishop e4 to dominate the center and target weak squares, then continue accumulating small advantages.

notes.explains: Pushing a5 and b4 is a classic queenside attack, aiming to smash through White's structure while the bishop on b1 is still holding the fort.
notes.teaches: In positions with a static bishop, a pawn storm on the opposite side can break through before the defender can reorganize.
notes.plans: Execute a5 and b4 to open lines on the queenside, targeting White's pawn structure.

notes.explains: If White captures on e4, the recapture with the pawn is correct because after dxe4, the knight on e3 forks the queen and rook, winning material.
notes.teaches: When the queen and rook are on the same rank one square apart, be alert for pawn forks that exploit that alignment.

notes.explains: The bishop on b1 cannot be captured because the queen on b2 protects it, and White's king move g2 is panic, allowing the bishop to take a pawn and collapse White's queenside structure.
notes.teaches: When a piece is defended indirectly (e.g., by a queen), it can become a powerful attacker that the opponent cannot easily remove.
notes.plans: Capture on b2 with the bishop, then exploit the resulting structural weaknesses on the queenside.

notes.explains: After sustained pressure, the opponent often collapses in one or two moves, making two huge blunders in a row.
notes.teaches: Consistent pressure over many moves can force even strong players into sudden mistakes; the 'game arc' of accumulating pressure leads to a rapid collapse.
notes.plans: Take the disciplined approach: capture with the bishop on e5, as it cannot be recaptured, and continue converting the advantage.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has two ways to win: a flashy approach or a solid, working man's approach. The disciplined choice is to take with the bishop on e5, because the bishop cannot be recaptured. After White's likely reply Ba4, Black has a pretty follow-up tactic that ends the game.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning tactical sequence, test different move orders. Sometimes switching the order makes the execution cleaner and more forcing.
notes.plans: Play Bxe5, then after Ba4, execute the tactic (e.g., Be3 forcing Qxe3, then Bxd4 attacking the queen with two defenders).

notes.explains: After taking the rook on f2, the rook on d1 is hanging. If White captures it, Black recaptures with the queen (not the rook) to maintain an x-ray against White's queen. If White plays Kxf2, Black has discovered checks to win the queen.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece to use to maintain threats. Keeping the x-ray or discovered attack can be more valuable than material equality.
notes.plans: Take on f2 with the rook, then if White captures the d1 rook, recapture with the queen to keep the x-ray. If White plays Kxf2, deliver a discovered check to win the queen.

notes.explains: In this obscure line of the Sicilian (Bc4 and a3), Black's best moves are Nf6, then e6, then d5. After e4 d5 exd5, the best move is not Bd6 but something more concrete, an idea that also occurs in the Jobava London.
notes.teaches: When facing unfamiliar opening lines, use engines and databases to learn the best moves. Concrete tactical ideas often repeat across different openings.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, e6, d5, and then find the concrete best move (likely a tactical shot) instead of automatic development.

notes.explains: After d4 cxd4, automatically recapturing with the pawn is a mistake because it allows White's minor pieces to develop freely. Instead, the correct idea is to leave the pawn on d3 and play Bg4, putting pressure on the knight on f3.
notes.teaches: In certain pawn structures, it is better to ignore a recapture and focus on rapid development and pressure, even at the cost of a pawn. The pawn on d3 can act as a barrier, burying White's minor pieces.
notes.plans: After Bg4, if White plays Ne2, then Bd6 completes the burial of White's pieces. Black can then attack the kingside with moves like Qb7, sacrificing more pawns to open lines, and eventually deliver a checkmate like the Anastasia's mate pattern.

notes.explains: The underlying problem for White throughout the sequence is that his queenside is not developed, leaving him unable to defend all the squares on the kingside. This paralysis allows Black to build a crushing attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down or undeveloped, you can often sacrifice material to open lines and create a direct attack on the king. The key is to recognize when the opponent cannot coordinate their defense.
notes.plans: In the given line, Black continues with moves like Rf8, Bc4, b5, and then Nf3+ forking the queen and rook, exploiting White's paralysis.

notes.explains: White's position is paralyzed because black has strong central control and active pieces, making it difficult for white to find constructive moves.
notes.teaches: Paralysis in chess occurs when one side has no useful moves, often due to a cramped position or threats that limit options. Recognizing when your opponent is paralyzed allows you to improve your position without rushing.
notes.plans: Black should continue improving piece placement, possibly with moves like ...Rc8 or ...Nd4, while waiting for white to weaken.

notes.explains: The move ...b5 attacks the bishop on c4, forcing it to move or be captured, and opens lines for black's pieces.
notes.teaches: Pawn breaks like ...b5 can create tactical threats and open lines, especially when the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated.
notes.plans: After ...b5, black can follow up with ...Bf3 and ...Nd4, forking the queen and rook, or simply win the bishop.

notes.explains: In this position, black has sacrificed material but has active pieces and white is paralyzed, making the pawn count irrelevant.
notes.teaches: Material is not always the most important factor; activity, coordination, and initiative can outweigh a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: Black should focus on maintaining pressure and exploiting white's lack of counterplay rather than trying to regain material immediately.

notes.explains: The move ...d4 is a central break that opens lines and creates threats, but in this case, black played ...Bg4 instead, which allowed white to play h3 and g4, gaining activity.
notes.teaches: Central pawn breaks like ...d4 are often critical in the Sicilian to open lines for the pieces and challenge white's center. Delaying such breaks can allow white to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Black should have played ...d4 to maintain pressure. After ...d4, black's pieces become more active, and white's position remains difficult.

notes.explains: In a Ruy Lopez game, black played a positional move to carve out d4 for a knight, but missed that ...Bh5 wins because the knight on f6 is pinned and undefended after gxh5.
notes.teaches: When a pawn moves past a square, it can open up a nasty pin. Always check if the piece that was defending a square is now undefended after a pawn capture.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Bh5, forcing gxh5, then ...Ba4 pins the knight on f6, winning material because the knight is undefended and the other knight is also pinned.

notes.explains: In this position, the knight on f3 is pinned, but black cannot exploit it directly because white can bring reserves to defend. The key is to involve another black piece to increase pressure.
notes.teaches: When a pin is not immediately decisive, look for ways to bring additional attackers to the pinned piece, often by opening lines or using tactical motifs like forks.
notes.plans: Black plays Rg8, threatening to open the g-file and create threats against the white king. After white's response, black can play Nh4, then g5, breaking the pin and winning material.

notes.explains: The move gxf6 is important because it opens the g-file, which keeps the black king safe and creates attacking chances. Playing Bxf6 would allow white to give check on e1 and win material.
notes.teaches: When considering captures, prioritize moves that open lines for your pieces and improve king safety, even if they seem less natural.
notes.plans: After gxf6, white may play Nd5, then black can play Nd4 or Rg8+ to exploit the open file and the weakness of h3.

notes.explains: In the position with a pin on the knight on f3, black cannot immediately exploit it because white can reinforce with a knight to d2. The solution is Rg8, which threatens to open the g-file and create a fork on g5.
notes.teaches: When a direct attack fails, use a rook lift to create threats that force weaknesses or overload the opponent's defenses.
notes.plans: After Rg8, if white plays Nb1, black can play Nh4, then g5, breaking the pin and winning. If white plays Nb-d2, black plays g4, threatening to take the knight and open lines.

notes.explains: Pins are powerful, especially when the pinned piece is unprotected. In the given line, after g4, if White captures the knight on h4, Black recaptures with the rook, exposing White's king to a devastating attack.
notes.teaches: A pin becomes crushing when the pinned piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable target, and the pinned piece lacks defenders.

notes.explains: The move Queen D7 can be a serious inaccuracy because it encourages g5 with tempo, after which White threatens to capture on f6 and then on d5, putting pressure on Black's center.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for your queen, consider whether it invites a pawn advance that gains time and creates threats against your position.
notes.plans: Black might need to play d4 to relieve pressure, but then White's knight retreats to e2 and later goes to f4, giving White a strong initiative.

notes.explains: Playing b5 in the Sicilian neutralizes the opponent's bishop by restricting its mobility, which unties your hands to act in the center.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to restrict your opponent's pieces. The concept of restriction is underrated but crucial for changing the course of the game.
notes.plans: After b5, follow up with c4 to further restrict the bishop and gain space.

notes.explains: In a complex position with no direct threats, retreating moves like Qc8 can be strong because they keep the status quo and improve the position subtly.
notes.teaches: Do not undervalue retreating moves; they can defuse threats and prepare tactics. Keeping the tension is often better than forcing the issue.
notes.plans: After Qc8, follow with ...g4 and ...Ne4 to exploit the weakened defense of the rook on d1.

notes.explains: In the line after ...Ne4, if White plays Nf5 instead of retreating the queen, Black must avoid the trap of ...exf5? because Rxc7 wins. Instead, Black plays Rd5! followed by Rd8, which refutes White's idea.
notes.teaches: In tactical sequences, constantly update your board state and look for counter-tactics. A quiet move like Rd5 can solve problems that aggressive recaptures cannot.
notes.plans: After Rd5 and Rd8, Black is winning.

notes.explains: In complex positions, every move must be evaluated by updating the board state, focusing on tactical strengths and weaknesses, especially which pieces become undefended. Here, after a rook move, the rook on d1 was poorly defended, with a black rook on d8 staring down the queen, making a tactic possible.
notes.teaches: Always ask: 'What pieces does this move leave undefended?' This helps spot tactical opportunities like forks or skewers.
notes.plans: After finding such a weakness, look for moves that exploit it, such as Rook d5 to attack the undefended rook and queen.

notes.explains: A retreating knight move (Knight g5) can be powerful if it opens up key squares. Here, moving the knight from f3 opened the d4 square, allowing a fork threat on the queen and king via knight d4 after recapturing with the pawn.
notes.teaches: Retreating knight moves are difficult but can create tactical opportunities by clearing lines or opening outposts. Look for squares like d4 that become accessible and can fork enemy pieces.
notes.plans: After Knight g5, if white takes, recapture with the pawn, then play Knight d4 forking the queen and rook, winning material.

notes.explains: White's move d4 was a mistake because it opened the diagonal for the black bishop, gave black a strong square on e4, and buried white's own bishop. It relinquished counterplay and made black's position dominant.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that open lines for the opponent's pieces or give them strong outposts without compensation. Keeping the tension with neutral moves (like King g2) can be better, forcing the opponent to find a plan.
notes.plans: Black should exploit the e4 square and the bishop's diagonal, possibly with Queen b8, Bishop e4, and doubling rooks on the e-file. White should protect the bishop on b1, e.g., with Rook ff1.

notes.explains: In this position, black's queenside play with a5-b4 is decisive because it opens a second front where black is already better, putting white under massive practical strain. White cannot trade bishops due to the threat of e3, and the c3 pawn is weak.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, opening a second front on the side where you are stronger can overwhelm the opponent's defense, even if the immediate tactical threats are minor.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press on the queenside, possibly simplifying to exploit the weak c3 pawn, while keeping an eye on tactical threats like e3.

notes.explains: The queen should often be used as a supporting piece, not the main attacker. In this game, the queen was moved to c8 to support from a distance, avoiding being a target and allowing other pieces to lead the attack.
notes.teaches: The queen is most effective as a 'supporting actress'—placed behind the scenes to reinforce threats without exposing itself. This counter-intuitive idea can be crucial in converting an attack.
notes.plans: Consider moving the queen to a safe square where it supports the attack indirectly, such as c8 or h6, rather than forcing it forward.

notes.explains: When deciding on a move, first determine the category of move you want to play (e.g., improving, aggressive, defensive). This narrows options and helps find good moves like Rook fe8 or a5, even if the best move is Queen c8.
notes.teaches: Start by deciding the type of move you need (e.g., improve piece, open a file), then look for specific candidates. This prevents tunnel vision and makes calculation easier.
notes.plans: In similar positions, first ask: 'What is my goal here?' Then find moves that fit that goal.

notes.explains: The queen on h6 is the best piece on the board, but a direct pawn attack like h4 is too slow because Black can generate counterplay with ...Be4, threatening the queen and making progress difficult.
notes.teaches: When a direct pawn storm is too slow, look to involve your minor pieces—especially knights—to break through. A queen alone with a rook often cannot force checkmate.
notes.plans: The plan is to reroute the knight via c5 and d3 to e5, using the queen on e3 to support the knight's journey and keep Black's queen tied down to f7.

notes.explains: The queen retreats to e3 not to defend, but to 'direct traffic'—it clears the way for the knight to go to c5, then d3, then e5, while also preventing Black's counterplay.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves can be powerful when they enable a better regrouping. The queen on e3 is a supporting piece, not the main attacker.
notes.plans: After the knight reaches e5, the winning idea is a retreating knight move to g4, attacking h6. Black must capture the pawn on h6, but then the queen goes to h3, and h6 is indefensible, leading to checkmate.

notes.explains: The winning move is not a direct capture or check, but a quiet knight retreat to g4. This attacks h6, and after Black takes the pawn, the queen delivers checkmate on h6.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the most effective attacking move is a retreat that opens new threats. Look for moves that improve your pieces' positions rather than forcing immediate material gain.

notes.explains: Against Nc3 in the Sicilian, black should play the same response they would against the open Sicilian (e.g., d6 for Najdorf players, e6 for Paulsen/Taimanov players). This avoids being move-ordered into a line they don't know.
notes.teaches: When white plays a non-open Sicilian move like Nc3, black can transpose back to their preferred open Sicilian by playing the corresponding move, preventing white from forcing an unfamiliar variation.
notes.plans: After Nc3, black should play their usual open Sicilian move (e.g., d6 or e6) to maintain familiarity.

notes.explains: For Accelerated Dragon players, an immediate …g6 against Nc3 is underrated and avoids the theoretical line with Nc6 Bb5. It has no major downside, and Bb5 is now pointless.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, if you play the Accelerated Dragon, consider …g6 against Nc3 to sidestep the Rossolimo (Bb5) lines and keep the game in your repertoire.
notes.plans: After …g6, black develops naturally, waiting for white's bishop placement before committing.

notes.explains: Against the Grand Prix Attack (white plays Bc4 and f4), black should avoid e6 because it allows white to trade knights and push e5, creating dark-square weaknesses on d6, f6, and c5. Instead, black can play ...d6 or the immediate ...Nd4, which exploits the vulnerability of white's bishop on c4.
notes.teaches: In the Grand Prix Attack, black should not play e6 early; instead, ...d6 or ...Nd4 are good responses. The move ...Nd4 is a common tactical idea when white's bishop is on c4, as it threatens to trade off white's key attacking piece.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Nd4, offering a trade of knights to remove white's light-squared bishop, which is the main attacker in the Grand Prix. After ...Nxb5, black recaptures and has a comfortable position.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack, White's light-squared bishop on c4 is a key attacker targeting f7. Black should trade it off when possible to neutralize White's main threat.
notes.teaches: When facing a dangerous attacking piece, trading it can be a good defensive strategy even if it costs a tempo.
notes.plans: After the trade, Black should focus on completing kingside development while keeping the knight on b5 in place for now.

notes.explains: Black should not rush to play a6 to chase the knight on b5, as the knight is not immediately threatening and is undefended. Playing a6 would allow it to retreat to c3, where it controls d5.
notes.teaches: Avoid automatic reactions like a6; consider whether the enemy piece is actually dangerous before driving it to a better square.
notes.plans: Instead, play d6 to control central squares and prepare to develop the knight to f6, preventing e5.

notes.explains: Black should not develop the bishop to d7 with tempo, as that helps White's knight return to c3. Instead, develop the knight to f6, which is more active and does not aid White's regrouping.
notes.teaches: Avoid giving the opponent free tempos that improve their piece placement; prefer developing moves that don't assist their plans.
notes.plans: After Nf6, if White plays e5, Black can capture and then move the knight to d5, a strong central outpost.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack, Black should consider delaying kingside castling to avoid becoming a target for White's typical attacking moves like Qh4, f5, Bh6, and Ng5.
notes.teaches: When facing a direct kingside attack, delaying castling or castling queenside can be a safer alternative, though it requires careful piece coordination.
notes.plans: Black can aim to castle queenside by first playing Bg4, which develops the bishop and prepares Qd8-d7 to hit the knight on b5 and enable queenside castling. If White plays e5, Black can capture and then play Nf6-d5, with the idea of castling kingside to defend f7 if needed.

notes.explains: In this Grand Prix Attack position, the bishop on g4 gives black the option to capture the knight on f3 at any time. The principled move e5 must be calculated, but after e5 dxe5, black can bring the knight to d5. White's knight on f3 might go to g5, threatening f7, but black can castle kingside and defend f7. Here white plays Qh4 instead.
notes.teaches: In the Grand Prix Attack, black's bishop on g4 is a flexible piece that can trade for the knight on f3 when needed. Always consider the principled central break e5 and be ready to meet knight maneuvers with accurate king safety.
notes.plans: Black should continue with the general plan: play Qd7, then eliminate the knight on f3 with Bxf3 before castling queenside to avoid the annoying Ng5 threat that would attack the bishop on g4 after h3.

notes.explains: After castling queenside, black's king is safer on b8 than c8 because the c-file may open. The king on b8 also guards a7 and can run to a8 if needed. Other useful improvements include h5 to restrict the white queen and create a stronghold on g4 for a knight, or h6 and g5 to open the g-file against white's king.
notes.teaches: After queenside castling, King b8 is an automatic safety move in many positions. Small positional improvements like h5 can restrict the opponent's pieces and create future attacking squares.
notes.plans: Consider playing Kb8, h5 (with ideas of Ng4 or Qg4 after a queen trade), or h6/g5 to open lines on the kingside. The position is double-edged; black must balance defense with counterplay.

notes.explains: White plays e5, forcing black to calculate. Black's instinct is to capture with dxe5, isolating the pawn. The knight can then go to g4, the juiciest square. After Ng4, white may grab the pawn on f7, but black has counterplay: at minimum, Bg7 and taking on c5 leads to an extremely double-edged position.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn break, capturing to isolate the pawn is often correct. The knight on g4 can be a powerful outpost, and even if white wins a pawn, black can get dynamic compensation.
notes.plans: Calculate dxe5, then Ng4. If white takes on f7, black can play Bg7 and recapture on c5, creating a chaotic but playable position with active pieces.

notes.explains: The knight on g4 is active but far from safe. White can grab the pawn on f7, leading to chaotic double-edged play. The position is so sharp that intuitive assessment is sufficient over deep calculation.
notes.teaches: When a position is extremely double-edged, you can rely on intuition rather than calculating every line. Double-edged is good—it means both sides have chances.
notes.plans: If White takes on f7, Black can consider checks on d4 or interposition tactics like Bishop to f6 to intercept the rook's defense of the queen.

notes.explains: A discovered check is only effective if the discovered piece cannot capture the checking piece. Here, after Rxf7, Qd4+ Kh1, the knight on g4 cannot give check on f2 because the queen on d4 is guarded by the rook on f7.
notes.teaches: When setting up a discovered check, ensure the piece you uncover against cannot capture the piece delivering the check. Otherwise, the tactic fails.
notes.plans: Interpose with Bishop to f6 to block the rook's defense, then Qd4+ and Nf2+ wins the queen. If the king goes to f1, Ne3+ also wins the queen.

notes.explains: After White plays h3, the knight on g4 must retreat. The best square is f6, where it trades off White's strongest piece—the centralized knight. After Nxf6 exf6 or Bxf6, White's bishop on c1 is undeveloped and tied to the b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks your active piece, consider retreating to trade off their strongest piece. A simplified position with a superior bishop can be a long-term advantage.
notes.plans: Play Qd4+ first to prevent Nxc5, then retreat the knight to f6. If White takes on f7, the check on d4 remains a threat.

notes.explains: The bishop on c1 is undeveloped and tied to defending the b2 pawn, making it a poor piece. Black's bishop is superior in a simplified position.
notes.teaches: When a piece is tied to defending a pawn, it becomes passive. Compare the activity of bishops to decide which side has the advantage.
notes.plans: Maintain pressure on White's weak pawns and exploit the passive bishop.

notes.explains: If White plays Be3 to intercept the check and protect the knight, Black can capture on e3 with the bishop, and then the queen replaces the bishop on e3, pinning the rook and keeping the knight protected.
notes.teaches: When an opponent interposes a piece, you can often replace it with a more valuable piece to maintain threats. The queen can fulfill two roles (protecting the knight and pinning the rook) if properly coordinated.
notes.plans: After Be3, play Bxe3, then Qxe3, maintaining the pin and the extra piece.

notes.explains: After winning a piece, Black should consider trading queens to simplify, following the 'one piece threshold rule': if up a piece or more, queen trades are beneficial. The knight on g4 is active but vulnerable; play h5 to prevent h3 from kicking it away, creating a 'fishing hook' idea.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by trading queens if possible. Prophylactic moves like h5 can protect an active piece from being harassed. Don't abandon ideas like e5 just because of obstacles; find a classy way to achieve them.
notes.plans: Play h5 to secure the knight, then consider trading queens or improving the bishop (e.g., Bd6 to exchange the annoying bishop on f4).

notes.explains: Black's king is restricted and vulnerable to checks or rook lifts on the c-file. The bishop on c5 is powerful but also a target; Black wants to neutralize it and give the king breathing room.
notes.teaches: When a specific plan (like e5) is blocked, don't abandon it—prepare it with the lowest-value piece. Using a pawn (f6) to prepare e5 is often better than using a piece because pawns are excellent at supporting other pawns.
notes.plans: Play f6, threatening g5 and preparing e5 to shut down the bishop and relieve the king's congestion.

notes.explains: After f6, White has no constructive moves because the threat of e5 is overwhelming. The position is highly charged with tactical tension, increasing the chance of blunders.
notes.teaches: In positions with high tactical tension, the side with more threats often forces errors. A move that shuts down the opponent's counterplay while creating multiple threats can be game-winning.
notes.plans: Follow up with e5 to immobilize the bishop and open lines; then target weaknesses like d3.

notes.explains: After White's counterplay is shut down, Black can finally play e5, making White's pieces useless. The queen is safe on b6, and Black will pile up on the d3 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are 'biting on granite' (have no targets), you can slowly improve and create new threats. Piling up on a weak pawn is a standard winning method.
notes.plans: Play e5, then if c3, drop the queen to b6 with tempo, and eventually break through on d3.

notes.explains: Black has just played e5, shutting down White's counterplay. White's pieces are biting on granite, meaning they have no real targets. Black plans to drop the queen back to b6 with tempo if White plays c3, then pile up on the d3 pawn to break through.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are poorly placed ('biting on granite'), you can often improve your position with a central pawn push like e5, then use queen maneuvers to create pressure on weak pawns.
notes.plans: If White plays c3, Black plays Qb6 with tempo, then doubles on the d3 pawn to win it.

notes.explains: Black considers taking on b2 with the queen, but must be careful of a trap: after Qxb2, White can play Rb4, threatening Rc4 forking queen and pawn on c2. However, Black can simply take the a2 pawn instead, and is safe because White has no mating attack (the b7 pawn protects the king) and White's back rank is weak.
notes.teaches: When calculating captures, always check for opponent's counterplay like rook forks. Also, a protected pawn on b7 can keep the king safe from back-rank mates, and a weak opponent back rank can be exploited later.
notes.plans: Black can take the a2 pawn safely, or play the more clinical Rc8 to force White to either trade rooks or allow c2 to be taken.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack, Black's move g6 (instead of Nc6) has a downside: White can play Qxd4, then after Nf6, White plays e5. This line is theoretically equal but sharp. With the knight on c3 instead of f3, the position transposes to a Dragon-like setup after ...Bg7, etc. In one game, Duda played Bc7? which was bad because it allowed Nf4, ruining Black's structure. The engine suggests Qa5 instead.
notes.teaches: When choosing a setup like g6 against the Grand Prix, be aware of the Qxd4 line. It's playable but requires theoretical knowledge. If you get a Dragon-like position, typical Dragon ideas apply. Avoid moving the bishop to c7 if it allows a knight to f4, damaging your pawn structure.
notes.plans: In the Dragon-like position, Black should play Qa5 to develop and maintain equality.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack, after e4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 g6 Nf3 Bg7 Bb5, the main line is …Nf6 6.0-0 0-0, but the engine prefers …Nd4. However, a sharp alternative is …d5, which looks like a blunder because of exd5, but after …a6 Nc3 Nf6, Black wins back the pawn with interest, gaining the bishop pair and a strong pawn on d5.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings like the Sicilian, a move that appears to lose a pawn can be a sound sacrifice if it leads to rapid development and positional compensation. Always calculate concrete lines before dismissing a move as a blunder.
notes.plans: After …d5 exd5 a6 Nc3 Nf6, Black will recapture on d5 with the knight, leaving White with a weak e5 pawn and Black with the bishop pair. Black should aim to pressure the e5 pawn and exploit White's awkward knight on c3.

notes.explains: If White avoids the pawn capture and plays e5 to close the center, Black can respond with …d4, restricting the White knight on c3 and preventing it from retreating to a good square. After …a6, the knight is forced to the awkward a3 square.
notes.teaches: When the center closes, a pawn push like d4 can restrict enemy pieces and force them to poor squares. This is a typical idea in the Grand Prix Attack and similar closed Sicilian setups.
notes.plans: After e5 d4, Black will follow up with a6 to chase the bishop and then target the knight on a3. Black's plan is to complete development and exploit White's misplaced pieces.

notes.explains: In a sharp Sicilian position, the move Bg7 can look like a blunder because of g4, threatening to win the knight on f6. However, Black has the counter-resource d5, which opens lines and creates threats. If White captures on d5, the knight on f6 can drop back, or if White plays Nxd5, then Bxg4 overloads the queen, which must defend the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, a seemingly winning threat like g4 can be met by a central counterstroke (d5) that shifts the focus. Always look for counterplay in the center when your pieces are attacked on the flank.
notes.plans: After Bg7 g4, Black plays d5, opening the center. If White captures on d5, Black recaptures with the knight or bishop, creating threats against White's queen and king. Black should continue to attack White's weakened pawn structure and exposed king.

notes.explains: In the same sharp position, Black also has the resource f5, which forces White's pawn on g4 to move or capture en passant, after which Black recaptures with the knight. This creates further weaknesses in White's kingside.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are under attack, look for pawn breaks that open lines and create counterplay. Moves like f5 and d5 can turn a defensive position into an attacking one.
notes.plans: After f5, Black will recapture on g4 with the knight, opening the g-file and targeting White's king. Black should coordinate the queen and rook for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack with White castling short, the queen often goes to h4 to launch a kingside attack. A sample line: Black attacks the knight, White retreats, Black attacks on the queenside, then White plays b5, leading to a devastating attack.
notes.teaches: The queen maneuver to h4 is a key attacking idea in the Grand Prix Attack, often leading to quick checkmates if Black is careless.
notes.plans: White aims for a direct kingside assault, while Black must be careful to defend and counter on the queenside.

notes.explains: In the game, after d6, d3, Nf6, Qe1, Black played Bg4 which was inaccurate and led to a slightly worse position. The engine prefers other moves like a6 or Nbd7.
notes.teaches: In the Grand Prix Attack, Black must be precise; inaccurate moves like Bg4 can quickly turn the position in White's favor.
notes.plans: Black should aim for solid development and counterplay, avoiding premature bishop sorties.

notes.explains: White can also play Bc4 followed by Ng5, the classic Botvinnik setup, which is another major line in the Grand Prix Attack. Alternatives like taking the knight are bad for White.
notes.teaches: The Botvinnik setup (Bc4, Ng5) is a key attacking system in the Grand Prix Attack, targeting f7.
notes.plans: Black must respond accurately, often with e6 or d5 to neutralize the threat.

notes.explains: In the Grand Prix Attack, White often launches a kingside assault with moves like f5, aiming to open lines against the black king. A typical pattern involves sacrificing the rook on f6 to force a checkmate on h7 or h8, as seen in games where Black's king is stuck in the center or has castled kingside.
notes.teaches: The Grand Prix Attack is a dangerous system where White's attack often culminates in a checkmate on h7. Key ideas include playing f5 to open the f-file, using the knight on g5 to target h7, and sacrificing material to deliver mate.
notes.plans: White should aim to push f5, follow up with Ng5, and look for tactical blows like Rxf6 or Bxh6 to break through Black's defenses.

notes.explains: Black can counter White's kingside attack by playing ...h6 to chase away the knight on g5, and if White captures, Black recaptures with the rook, opening the h-file for a counterattack. This can turn the tables, as Black's own kingside assault becomes overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When facing a kingside attack, a timely ...h6 can deflect the knight and open lines for a counterattack. The h-file becomes a powerful weapon for the defending side if White's attack is premature.
notes.plans: Black should consider ...h6 to challenge the knight on g5, followed by ...g5 to blast open the kingside, using the rook and bishop to target White's king.

notes.explains: In this position, White played e5 prematurely, opening the center without sufficient development. This weakens White's king and allows Black to exploit the open lines with moves like Qd4, targeting the exposed white monarch.
notes.teaches: Opening the center too early when underdeveloped can backfire, as it gives the opponent chances to attack the king. Development and king safety should be prioritized before central breaks.
notes.plans: White should have considered a move like f5 to open the diagonal for the bishop while keeping the center closed, rather than playing e5.

notes.explains: Opening the center with e5 is premature when white is underdeveloped and the king is weak. Black should not rush to open lines without being ready.
notes.teaches: Do not open the center when your opponent is better developed; it exposes your own king.
notes.plans: White should consider f5 to open a diagonal for the bishop, or Bd2 to develop and avoid Ng4. Black can play ...Kb8 and ...Rb8 to prepare b5.

notes.explains: After e5, white can play Rxf7, leading to complications. Black's idea of Bf6 to win the queen fails because white has a monster pawn on e7 and active moves like Kg1, g3, chasing the queen away from defending the rook on c7.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing the queen, ensure you have enough compensation (pawns, active pieces) and that the opponent's queen can be driven away from key defenders.
notes.plans: White can play Kg1, then g3 to chase the queen, leaving black paralyzed despite extra material.

notes.explains: White has a drawing move: Be3 Qxe3+ Kh1, threatening smothered mate, but it's not actually smothered because the queen on h4 prevents it. Black cannot deliver effective discoveries; Ng4 is harmless.
notes.teaches: Do not apply tactical patterns blindly; verify they work in the specific position. Smothered mate requires the queen to be absent from h4.
notes.plans: Black should avoid Bf6 and instead trade white's only active piece with Rc8, leading to a winning attack after Rxc8 Qxc8, with unstoppable Qd4.

notes.explains: The correct move for black is Rc8, trading rooks. After Rxc8 Qxc8, black's queen and knight create a deadly attack against white's king, with Qd4 unstoppable.
notes.teaches: Trade your opponent's strongest active piece to reduce their counterplay and amplify your own attack.
notes.plans: Black plays Rc8, then after exchange, Qd4 threatens mate and wins.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has a powerful attack against White's king. The rook on f8 and the queen on d4 create unstoppable threats. White is forced to lose material.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is exposed, you should look for forcing moves that bring more pieces into the attack, even if it means sacrificing material temporarily.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press the attack, using the queen and rooks to create threats. The immediate plan is to play ...Qd4, threatening ...Qxf2# or ...Rxf2.

notes.explains: After White's mistake, Black has a winning position. The move ...Rc8 is incredibly strong, forcing White to take, after which Black recaptures and has a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and the opponent's king is weak, you should look for ways to simplify while maintaining the attack. Sometimes a direct rook sacrifice opens lines.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Rc8, and after White captures, recapture with the rook, then bring the queen to d4 with overwhelming threats.

notes.explains: White tried to defend with h3, but Black can play ...Nf6, threatening ...Ng4. However, White has ...Ne5, so Black should first play ...Bd4, then ...Nf6 or even better ...f5, counterattacking in the center.
notes.teaches: When calculating tactics, always consider intermediate moves (intermezzos) that improve your position before committing to a plan. A preliminary move can prevent the opponent's counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Bd4 first, then decide between ...Nf6 and ...f5, both of which maintain the attack.

notes.explains: After ...Bxe3, Black can play ...Bxc3+ (replacement idea), then ...Qd4, defending the knight and attacking the rook, winning a full rook.
notes.teaches: The replacement idea: when a piece is attacked, you can sometimes sacrifice it to bring a more powerful piece to the same square, creating new threats.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Bxc3+ first, then ...Qd4, winning material.

notes.explains: In a winning position, Black should avoid unnecessary complications. For example, instead of ...Rc4+ (which allows counterplay), just take on a2 and win. If White tries checks, Black can hide the king with ...Kb8 and block with the queen.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, choose the simplest path to victory. Avoid giving the opponent counterplay. If checks come, you can often hide the king and block with pieces to prevent perpetual check.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Rxa2, winning a pawn and simplifying. If White checks, move the king to b8 and block with the queen.

notes.explains: In many openings, a common checkmate pattern occurs on the h5-f7 diagonal, such as the 1620 game with Knight h5 and Bishop g6 mate.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for checkmate patterns along the h5-f7 diagonal, especially when the opponent weakens their kingside.

notes.explains: Against the Hippo setup (double fianchetto), the recommended approach is to grab the center with d4 and play Bishop d6, avoiding Knight c6 in favor of c6 to blunt the opponent's king's bishop.
notes.teaches: In symmetrical setups like the Hippo, prioritize controlling the center and placing pawns to neutralize enemy bishops.
notes.plans: Continue developing with c6, then fianchetto or castle as needed.

notes.explains: When White plays f4, it is a weakening move. Instead of entering tactical complications (e.g., exf4, Bxg7, fxg3 sacrificing a rook), a simple positional response is Knight c6, protecting the e5 pawn. The old setup (c6) can be discarded because f4 changes the priorities.
notes.teaches: Be flexible: when the opponent makes a weakening move, adapt your plan. Prioritize protecting key pawns over following a preset setup.
notes.plans: After Knight c6, White may trade on e5; recapture with the pawn, freeing f6 for the knight, then castle kingside, eliminating any weaknesses.

notes.explains: Playing f6 might seem anti-positional (violating the 'never play f6' rule), but here it is concrete: White's pieces are far from the black kingside, so the weakness is temporary. After White trades on e5, black recaptures with the pawn, vacating f6 for the knight, and castles, leaving no trace of weakness.
notes.teaches: Concrete assessment overrules general principles. A weakening move like f6 can be safe if the opponent cannot exploit it immediately.
notes.plans: After f6, allow White to capture on e5, recapture with the pawn, play Nf6, then castle kingside.

notes.explains: When White plays d4, it creates weaknesses in White's camp, blunts their bishops, and yields center control. The standard response is to push e4, gaining space and opening lines.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their center, advance your own pawns to exploit the weaknesses and restrict their pieces.
notes.plans: Push e4, then continue developing with active piece play against White's compromised position.

notes.explains: White has yielded central control and created weaknesses, particularly on e3. The bishop on g2 is passive, and the pawn chain is ideal for Black. The knight on h4 is trapped because the bishop controls f5, and g5 can trap it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates weaknesses in their camp, exploit them by targeting weak squares (like e3) and trapping pieces. A trapped knight can be won with a pawn push if the escape squares are controlled.
notes.plans: Push e4 to attack the center and open lines, then play g5 to trap the knight on h4. After winning the piece, consider castling or launching a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After the Greek Gift, Black can win quickly by pushing e3 to block the king's escape square, then deliver checkmate with queen and rook.
notes.teaches: When delivering checkmate, block the king's escape squares (like e3) to force mate. Efficiency matters: choose the fastest sequence to avoid counterplay.
notes.plans: Push e3 to block the king's escape, then use queen and rook to deliver checkmate. No need to calculate further; the win is straightforward.

notes.explains: In a mating attack, the king's escape square is d2, so blocking it with e3 is more efficient than checking with Qf2, which would allow the king to flee.
notes.teaches: When delivering checkmate, first identify the king's only escape route and block it, rather than just giving checks.
notes.plans: After e3, follow up with Qd3 to threaten mate, forcing a quick finish.

notes.explains: In the Hippo/Owens Defense (e4 g6 Nf3 c3? ... e6), the old line e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 a3 ... f5? is a mistake; White wins by taking en passant (exf6). If Black recaptures with Bxg2, White checks on h5 and Black's best defense is Bg7, not Nf6 (which allows a quick mate).
notes.teaches: The en passant capture exf6 in the Owens Defense leads to a winning attack; Black's correct defense is Bg7, not Nf6, to avoid a quick mate on the h5-e8 diagonal.
notes.plans: After exf6 Bxg2, play Qh5+; if Black plays Bg7, continue with gxh7+ Kf8, then the key move is Nh3 (not taking the knight) to reroute to g5, threatening mate. Black must play Nh6 to defend, and White continues with a plan to deliver mate or win material.

notes.explains: The mate on the h5-e8 diagonal (e.g., Qh5, Bg6#) appears in many openings: the From's Gambit (f4 e5 fxe5 d6 exd6 Bxd6 Nf3 g5? g3? or Qg3? ...) and the Dutch Defense (d4 f5 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5? Bg3 f4 e3! threatening Qh5#).
notes.teaches: Be alert for the early checkmate pattern on the h5-e8 diagonal in various openings; it often arises when Black weakens the kingside with pawn moves like g5 or f4.
notes.plans: In such positions, consider moves like e3 to open the diagonal for the queen and bishop, delivering mate if Black captures the bishop.

notes.explains: In the Owen's Defense, after White takes the pawn on d5, the knight should go to h3, not capture the pawn. This prepares the knight to go to g5, threatening checkmate on h7. Black's only defense is ...Nh6, which paralyzes Black's position.
notes.teaches: When you have a direct mating threat, prioritize the attack over material. The knight on h3 is a key redeployment to g5, and you should not be distracted by capturing pawns.
notes.plans: After Black plays ...Nh6, White develops the queenside with Nc3, Bd2, and castles queenside. Then the rook on a1 joins the attack via g1. White slowly builds up while Black is helpless.

notes.explains: Once the rook is on g1, White threatens to open the g-file. If Black tries to defend with the queen, White can eliminate the bishop on h6 and redeploy the knight to f3, then to h4, aiming for g6. Black is completely helpless.
notes.teaches: In a positional crush, you don't need to rush. Slowly improve your pieces and bring your rook into the attack. The knight can be redeployed to create new threats.
notes.plans: Play Rg1, then if Black defends, take on h6, drop the knight back to f3, and prepare to infiltrate via g6 with the rook. The knight eventually goes to h4 to access g6.

notes.explains: In a different game, White played a setup with g3, Bb2, and f4. Black responded with ...e5, ...d5, ...Bd6, and ...exf4. White then played h4 to prevent the queen from entering the attack, but the rook on h1 becomes vulnerable. The position becomes messy.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a dangerous attacking setup, you can blunt their bishop with ...f6 and develop your knight to f6, forcing them to release tension. Avoid creating weaknesses like d3 that give your opponent targets.
notes.plans: Black should castle, then threaten ...e4, play ...Qd7 and ...Bh3. White's position is passive and Black controls the center. If White plays d4, Black responds ...e4 and after Nh4, ...g5 ends the game.

notes.explains: After White plays Ne5, Black should not trade the dark-squared bishop for the knight. Instead, castle and keep the bishop. Trading would give White the d2 square for the queen and allow White to protect the kingside.
notes.teaches: Don't give up a powerful bishop for a knight just to win a pawn or simplify. Keep your pieces that are active and control key squares. Patience is often better than forcing trades.
notes.plans: Black castles, keeps the bishop, and maintains pressure. White's position remains passive.

notes.explains: After Black's Knight E5, the most resilient move is to castle rather than trade the dark-squared bishop for the knight. Trading would activate White's pieces and leave Black's king in the center.
notes.teaches: Don't give up a strong bishop for a knight just to win a pawn if it activates the opponent's pieces and leaves your king vulnerable. Simple development and king safety are more important.
notes.plans: Castle, then chase the knight away with Queen E7 or Queen E8. After Queen E8, trade queens and redeploy the queen to H5 for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: In the Glek system, after Black plays A6, White should not play A4 because it weakens the B4 square. Instead, continue development with Bishop G2.
notes.teaches: Don't make prophylactic pawn moves that weaken key squares unless necessary. Focus on development and wait for Black's decision.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to G2 and await Black's dark-squared bishop placement.

notes.explains: After Black plays Bishop B4, White should not play D3 to defend the pawn because Black isn't threatening to win it. Instead, castle and recapture with the d-pawn if Black takes on C3.
notes.teaches: Don't play defensive moves out of fear; check if the threat is real. Recapturing with the d-pawn opens lines and maintains central control.
notes.plans: Castle, and if Black captures on C3, recapture with the d-pawn.

notes.explains: After Black captures on C3, the standard tactical response is Knight takes E5, discovering an attack on the knight. This wins back the pawn immediately.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical blows that exploit the opponent's pinned or loose pieces. Knight takes E5 is a typical idea when the opponent's knight is undefended.
notes.plans: Play Knight takes E5, then recapture the bishop. White is better due to the bishop pair, Black's king in the center, and piece mobility.

notes.explains: The knight on c4 is loose and can be targeted. Queen to e2 attacks the knight and sets up a discovered check threat with Bxb7, winning the rook on a8. Black's best defense is Be6, but then f5 wins the bishop.
notes.teaches: When a knight is undefended and the opponent's king is exposed, look for moves that combine direct threats with tactical motifs like discovered attacks.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, threatening Bxb7 and a discovered check. If Black plays Be6, push f5 to win the bishop. If Black plays Nb6, take on b7 and win the exchange.

notes.explains: After winning the exchange, White should simplify by trading queens and then capturing the rook. The order of operations matters: take the rook first, then win the bishop with f5.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, prioritize material gain and simplify to a technically winning endgame. Avoid unnecessary complications unless you are certain of the outcome.
notes.plans: Take the rook on a8, then play f5 to win the bishop. After that, activate the bishop to a safe square like f4, bring the rook into play, and trade rooks to ease conversion.

notes.explains: With a full rook advantage, White can proceed methodically: activate the bishop, bring the rook to the seventh rank, and restrict the enemy king. Black's attempts like g5 or Kh7 are harmless.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, focus on activating your pieces, restricting the opponent's king, and trading down to a simpler win. Patience and prophylaxis are key.
notes.plans: Play Re8, then Rf5, and bring the other rook to e7. If Black plays Nd5, drop the bishop back to e3 and later redeploy to d4. Alternatively, push h4 to restrict the king and set up checkmate threats.

notes.explains: We are up material, so we can ignore tripled pawns and just capture weak pawns like c4. The conversion is straightforward: push the d-pawn, make a queen, and deliver checkmate (e.g., Rook d4, Rook f4, Queen d3, Rook f1 mate).
notes.teaches: When converting a winning endgame, prioritize cleanliness over speed. Avoid unnecessary counterplay by identifying and capturing weak pawns, and always be aware of stalemate possibilities.
notes.plans: Push the d-pawn to promote, then use the queen and rooks to deliver checkmate, ensuring no stalemate tricks.

notes.explains: In the Glek system, after e4, Black's a6 is not a main line but not terrible if Black develops the bishop. The main lines are Bishop c5 (most popular) and d5 (second main line, leading to an early exchange and a typical Glek pawn structure). After Bishop c5, Bishop g2 contains a trap: if Black castles, White has Knight takes c5 (center fork trick) and after d4, Black must play Bishop d6 to maintain the bishop. After de, Bishop e5, we castle, allowing Bishop takes c3—we don't fear queenside pawn damage; we want the bishop pair and dark-square control.
notes.teaches: In the Glek system, prioritize the bishop pair and dark-square control over queenside pawn structure. The center fork trick (Knight takes c5) is a key resource after Bishop c5.
notes.plans: If Black plays d6 instead of Bishop d6, White has a strong prophylactic move: Knight e2, preparing f4 to trap the bishop. Black's best is Knight d7, but then White gets a kingside initiative with f4, g4, g5, and Knight to g3/f5.

notes.explains: After Bb4, White responds with Bg2 and is not afraid of early captures on e4 because Nxe5 is a strong reply. If Black avoids the capture and plays d6, a good setup is Qe2 followed by b3, Bb2, and c4 to create a central bind. The bishop on b2 controls d4, and White can improve the kingside with h3, Kh2, and Nh4. The move Bg4 is not feared because h3 can be played, and if the bishop retreats to h5, White can ignore it and continue with Nh4 and Nf5.
notes.teaches: In the Hippo/Glek setups, early captures on e4 are not dangerous if you have a tactical response like Nxe5. When Black delays captures, building a central bind with b3, Bb2, and c4 is a strong plan, and the bishop on b2 is well-placed to control key central squares.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, then b3, Bb2, and c4 to pressure the center. Improve the kingside with h3, Kh2, and Nh4, aiming for Nf5. If Black plays Bg4, simply push h3 and continue the plan.

notes.explains: After Nxc4, White recaptures with Nxc5, which is a typical tactic. The recapture dxc3 is preferred over bxc3 because it increases central control and opens the bishop. However, bxc3 is also playable and sometimes necessary, e.g., if Black plays d5, then bxc3 is correct to avoid a queen trade.
notes.teaches: When recapturing with a pawn, prefer the pawn that improves central control and opens lines for your pieces. Evaluate each capture based on the resulting pawn structure and piece activity.
notes.plans: After Nxc5, continue development and maintain central pressure. If recapturing with a pawn, choose dxc3 when possible to strengthen the center.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian Exchange variation, the move Nxe5 is unwise because of Nxe4, similar to a trick in the Glek system where Nxf7 can be met by taking the knight with the bishop and then capturing on f7.
notes.teaches: Recognize tactical patterns where a knight capture on e5 or f7 can be refuted by a counter-capture that wins a piece.

notes.explains: Pushing the f-pawn to f5 is a key idea. If the knight reroutes to f6, Bg5 pins it; if Black plays h6, the bishop retreats to h4, maintaining the pin. Black cannot easily escape the pin because of the threat of ...g5? and the queen's absence allows kingside attacks.
notes.teaches: A pawn push to f5 combined with a bishop pin on the knight can create a lasting bind, especially when Black's king is uncastled.
notes.plans: Continue pushing the f-pawn and use the pin to restrict Black's pieces, eventually opening lines against the king.

notes.explains: If Black castles, White can still play f6 to open the file and follow with Bg5, threatening to take the knight and expose the king. The tactical potential of the Glek system is high because all pieces aim at the kingside.
notes.teaches: Even after castling, a pawn break like f6 can open lines for a devastating attack when pieces are coordinated against the king.
notes.plans: Play f6 to open the f-file, then Bg5 to pin and capture the knight, leaving the king vulnerable.

notes.explains: Bg4 is not scary because the queen can slide to e1. Black's uncastled king suffers consequences. Against other moves, White pushes f5. Knight c4 is bad because Qe2 wins material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is uncastled, centralize the queen to defend and counter threats, while continuing the pawn advance.
notes.plans: Respond to Bg4 with Qe1; otherwise push f5. Exploit Black's lack of castling to gain time and space.

notes.explains: Even when up material, always check for threats like forks. In this game, if Black played Ne5, White would respond with Rf1 to avoid a fork.
notes.teaches: Never relax when ahead; always verify basic tactics like forks and checks to avoid blunders.
notes.plans: After winning material, consolidate by trading rooks and finding safe squares for the bishop, while remaining alert to counterplay.

notes.explains: After e4 c5, White plays c4, creating a hole on d4. Black should not assume this move loses; it's a legitimate sideline with venom if White follows up accurately.
notes.teaches: Avoid dismissing unusual moves as bad just because they look ugly; they may be playable and require respect.
notes.plans: Black should clamp down on d4 with Nc6, avoid e5, and choose a pawn structure (e.g., g6 or e6) to increase control over d4.

notes.explains: Black plays g6 to fianchetto the bishop, increasing control over d4. This is a standard setup independent of the specific Sicilian variation. The knight on g8 can go to f6 or e7 (Botvinnik setup); the latter keeps the long diagonal unobstructed and cooperates with the bishop.
notes.teaches: In closed Sicilian positions, fianchettoing the bishop is logical regardless of the exact variation. The Botvinnik setup (knight on e7) can be a harmonious alternative to Nf6.
notes.plans: Start with d6, then decide knight placement based on White's moves. Consider initiating favorable trades to increase control over d4.

notes.explains: Combining e6 and g6 in the Sicilian is usually a cardinal sin because it weakens d6, but in this closed center position, White cannot exploit d6, so the principle does not apply.
notes.teaches: General principles (like avoiding e6+g6 in the Sicilian) are context-dependent. Always evaluate whether the specific position allows exceptions.
notes.plans: Continue with h6 to ask the bishop's intentions, then respond accordingly.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian position with a closed center, the usual warning against combining e6 and g6 does not apply because White cannot access the d6 square. The closed center changes the evaluation of such setups.
notes.teaches: Principles that apply in open positions (like avoiding certain pawn structures) may be irrelevant in closed positions. Always reassess based on the specific pawn structure and piece activity.
notes.plans: Black can continue developing with h6 and Bh4, maintaining the clamp on d4.

notes.explains: Playing g5 is not about starting a pawn storm but about carving out the g6 square for the knight, emphasizing dark-square play. White's bishop on h4 is not a real tactical threat; Black can respond with Nf4, aiming for opposite-colored bishops to exploit White's dark-square weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn move like g5 is purely positional—to create an outpost for a knight. Opposite-colored bishops can turn a small positional edge into a lasting advantage by highlighting weaknesses on one color.
notes.plans: After a6 pushes the knight back to c3, Black recaptures on f4 with the bishop, then immediately reassesses the new position to find the queen on g5, adding pressure and eyeing the g-file.

notes.explains: With the queen on g5 and White panicking, Black can choose between Nd4 or Ne5. Nd4 is more thematic, occupying an outpost. White is on the verge of collapse. Black then plays Rg8, a non-threatening but preparatory move that builds up the attack without immediate tactics.
notes.teaches: Building an attack often involves 'mysterious' rook moves that don't threaten anything directly but bring pieces into optimal positions. Patience and gradual improvement can create threats that materialize later.
notes.plans: Black continues by moving the bishop to e5 to clear the g-file and prevent White from seeking counterplay with a4. The king stays in the center as it is safe, but castling queenside is an option if needed.

notes.explains: Black's Rook G8 doesn't create an immediate threat but improves piece coordination and builds pressure on the g-file. The idea is to prepare an attack by repositioning pieces to dominant squares.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, moves that don't threaten directly can still be strong if they improve your piece placement and set up future threats. Building an attack often requires patience and gradual accumulation of force.
notes.plans: Black aims to play Bishop to E5 to dominate dark squares and clear the way for doubling rooks on the g-file. Long castles is also a priority to secure the king and enable sacrifices.

notes.explains: White's Knight E2 would be a blunder because it obstructs the queen-bishop connection and allows a tactical shot. Black should be alert to such defensive mistakes.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong bind on dark squares, watch for opponent moves that block key defensive lines. A seemingly natural move like Knight E2 can be punished tactically.
notes.plans: Black can continue with long castles and then consider sacrifices or mating operations. The immediate threat is to exploit the pinned bishop or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: A tactical idea like Rook G3 (sacrifice) might be tempting but fails because after Hxg3, Fxg3, White's king escapes via light squares to E2. The evacuation route makes checkmate difficult.
notes.teaches: Always check if the opponent's king has an escape route before committing to a sacrifice. A rook sacrifice is only sound if the king cannot flee or if the attack is overwhelming.
notes.plans: Avoid unnecessary sacrifices; instead, play Rook G5 and follow up with Rook takes G2, which leads to checkmate. Rook H5 is also strong, threatening H3 and forcing resignation if White plays H3.

notes.explains: The move C4 in the Sicilian is not a mistake per se, but it requires precise follow-up. Grandmasters can play it because they know the plans, but lower-rated players often mishandle it and get crushed.
notes.teaches: Some opening moves are only good if you understand the resulting positions deeply. Playing a sharp line without preparation can backfire badly. It's better to stick to solid, principled development unless you know the theory.
notes.plans: If White plays C4 without a plan, Black can punish with standard development (Knight C6, G6) and then exploit White's weaknesses. The main line for White is G3 to fianchetto and control the center.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian setup with c5, Nc3, g6, the main line involves g3 and Bg2, leading to a position where Black is comfortable but White is not worse if accurate. Black's typical plan is queenside expansion with a6 and b5.
notes.teaches: In many anti-Sicilian setups (closed Sicilian, King's Indian Attack), Black's standard plan is to play a6 and b5 to start a queenside pawn storm.
notes.plans: Black should aim for a6, Rb8, and b5 to expand on the queenside, while being aware of tactical pitfalls like e5 if b5 is played prematurely.

notes.explains: When White plays h3 or f4, Black must avoid playing b5 immediately because e5 wins a piece. Instead, Black should first play Rb8 to get out of the pin, or consider Knight to e8 with ideas of rerouting to c7, e6, d4, and targeting a5 if White plays a5.
notes.teaches: Before playing b5 in such positions, always move the rook to b8 to avoid the e5 tactic. If White plays a5, the knight can maneuver to pick off the a5 pawn.
notes.plans: Black should play Rb8, then b5, or if White plays a5, reroute the knight via e8-c7-e6-d4 to attack the a5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black should generally avoid playing Nd4 if it requires recapturing with a pawn, because the d4 pawn becomes a weakness and the bishop on g7 is strong. Even if recapturing with the bishop is possible, it's often not a positive transformation.
notes.teaches: In positions with a fianchettoed bishop on g7, avoid placing a knight on d4 if it can be recaptured by a pawn, as that creates a weak pawn and reduces the bishop's scope.

notes.explains: In the Sicilian, Black often places the bishop on g7 and the knight on f6. The move Knight d4 is typically undesirable if Black must recapture with a pawn, because the resulting pawn on d4 becomes a weakness while White gains easy kingside expansion. Even if recapture with the bishop is possible, the knight on d4 is rarely positive unless Black can recapture with a knight.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing a knight on d4 in the Sicilian if you cannot recapture with a knight, as it creates a weak pawn and gives White free play on the kingside.
notes.plans: Instead, keep the bishop on g7 and maintain flexibility. Consider moves like Rook b8 or other developing moves that preserve the pawn structure.

notes.explains: When White plays Bishop e3 and Queen d2, Black can push b5 and then play Knight d4, which is now good because White cannot recapture with a knight. If White recaptures with the bishop, Black gains control of many dark squares. After Knight d1, Bc8-d7, e6-e5, Black has a strong pawn on d4 and the b-file for pressure.
notes.teaches: Knight d4 becomes a strong move when White cannot recapture with a knight, especially if it leads to dark-square control and a central pawn wedge.
notes.plans: Maintain the tension on the queenside with b5, avoiding b4 unless White has a pawn on c3. Keep the option of Bc8-b7 and later b5xc4 to win the b2 pawn. If White does not play Bishop e3, use Queen a5, Knight c7, Knight d4 to maneuver until an opportune moment for b5xc4.

notes.explains: After White plays Bishop g5, Black can play Knight g6 and then Bishop h5, Knight f4, targeting the dark squares. If White plays Queen g4, Black must be careful: the threat is Queen takes e6 (and also Queen takes c6). The correct defense is Queen f6, which covers both threats. King f8 is not good because it loses the pawn on f4. White can equalize with Knight d2, but Black should still be fine.
notes.teaches: When facing multiple threats from the queen, look for a defensive move that covers all critical squares. Here Queen f6 defends e6 and c6 simultaneously.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring White's dark squares and consider pushing b5 or playing Knight e5 to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In this position, Black faces multiple threats including a fork and Queen takes e6. The correct defensive move is Queen f6, covering both threats and maintaining the initiative.
notes.teaches: When under multiple threats, prioritize moves that address all threats simultaneously, often by centralizing the queen or coordinating pieces.
notes.plans: After Queen f6, Black can aim for King e7 to coordinate rooks and maintain pressure on the dark squares.

notes.explains: Black has compensation for a pawn due to total dark square control. White's Knight f4 was incautious; Black can exploit with Knight e5, maintaining dark-square dominance.
notes.teaches: Dark square control can provide lasting compensation for material, restricting the opponent's pieces and enabling attacking plans.
notes.plans: Continue to press on dark squares, possibly with Bishop e5 and long castling to bring the second rook into play.

notes.explains: If White plays Queen g4, Black can simply castle kingside, then bring the queen to g5, preserving all advantages. The plan remains Rook b8 and b5 to engineer a queenside attack.
notes.teaches: Castling can be a simple and effective way to neutralize threats while maintaining a positional edge. Stick to your plan even when the opponent tries to disrupt it.
notes.plans: Execute the queenside attack with Rook b8 and b5, exploiting the dark-square control.

notes.explains: Bishop takes b2 is a strong move, but the decision to avoid it was a general reluctance to allow queenside play. After Bishop e5, there is no queenside play, so taking is fine.
notes.teaches: When evaluating captures, consider whether they open lines for the opponent. If the resulting position is safe, the capture is often good.
notes.plans: If Bishop takes b2, follow up with Bishop e5 to control dark squares and prevent counterplay.

notes.explains: A beautiful but unnecessary queen sacrifice (Queen takes g2) leads to mate if ignored, but if White gives back the queen, Knight h4 forks bishop and knight. However, the simpler move (Knight takes f3) is fine.
notes.teaches: Avoid overly fancy moves unless you are certain they lead to mate. Simple, solid play is often better. Also, remember that mating threats can be parried by moves like Rook d1 that open escape routes for the king.
notes.plans: If you see a flashy sacrifice, calculate thoroughly. If it doesn't force a win, prefer the safe continuation.

notes.explains: In a similar position (Wolf–Andersson), Black defended with King g8 against the threat of mate on h7, avoiding the trap of h6 which would allow Bishop takes h6. Black survived because the center is closed and the king can escape.
notes.teaches: When defending against mate, consider king moves that avoid opening lines. A closed center can allow the king to flee to safety.
notes.plans: If the opponent threatens mate, look for defensive king moves that keep the position closed and prevent the attacker from bringing reinforcements.

notes.explains: In a kingside attack, the defender often tries to escape with the king to safety. Even when it looks like the attack is decisive, the king can sometimes flee to the center or the other wing and survive.
notes.teaches: The king can often escape on its own two feet; don't assume a king trapped on the kingside is doomed if there are escape routes.

notes.explains: When attacking, a rook lift to the third rank (e.g., Rg3) can be used to chase away the defending queen, opening up lines for mate. The rook cannot be captured due to a pin.
notes.teaches: A rook on the third rank can harass the queen and create mating threats, especially when combined with a pin on the g-file.
notes.plans: After chasing the queen away, capture on g2 or deliver mate with queen takes h3.

notes.explains: In a typical Sicilian structure, the plan is to advance the b-pawn to b5 and b4, targeting the c3 pawn. This is often preceded by moves like Bg4 pinning the knight and Nd7 reinforcing control over d4.
notes.teaches: The b5-b4 advance is a standard positional operation in many Sicilian lines, putting pressure on White's queenside and potentially opening lines.
notes.plans: Play b5, then b4, possibly supported by Nd7 to make the advance more effective by attacking the c3 pawn.

notes.explains: After White played Qe3, the alignment of the king and queen on the same diagonal with a bishop of that color triggers a tactical alert. The move f4 exploits this alignment, threatening to win the queen if White captures.
notes.teaches: Always be alert when the opponent's king and queen are on the same diagonal as your bishop; that alignment can create immediate tactical threats.
notes.plans: Play f4 to exploit the diagonal alignment, forcing White to give up a pawn or lose the queen.

notes.explains: Instead of capturing on b2 immediately (which allows White to recapture with the bishop), Rb8 is stronger because it paralyzes White by stopping Bc4 and threatening cxb2, increasing pressure on the dark squares.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for moves that restrict the opponent's options and maximize your piece activity rather than grabbing material immediately.
notes.plans: Play Rb8 to maintain pressure, then follow up with Qa5 to attack a2 and prepare further queenside advances.

notes.explains: With Qa5, the queen makes contact with the rook on e1, setting up tactical possibilities. If White plays Qxc2, the rook on e1 is undefended except for the knight on f3, which can be eliminated by Nd4. After Bxd4, White's best is Bb3, but otherwise c2 works, forcing Rb2 and White collapses.
notes.teaches: When your queen aligns with an enemy rook on the same file, look for ways to eliminate defenders (like the knight) to create tactical threats.
notes.plans: Consider Nd4 to remove the knight defender, then push c2 to exploit the undefended rook.

notes.explains: In a winning position, two main conversion methods are: open files and infiltrate with rooks, or push a passed pawn. Here, pushing c4 opens the b-file for the rook, which is the easiest way to convert.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, focus on either opening files for rooks or advancing passed pawns; choose the simplest method that creates immediate threats.
notes.plans: Play c4 to open the b-file, then use the rook to infiltrate and win more material.

notes.explains: When considering g5 to force a queen trade, first ensure the h6 square is protected. Using the king to control h6 is a reliable method, as the king can fulfill basic defensive tasks without risking tactical blunders like blocking the queen's connection.
notes.teaches: In endgames, don't forget the king can be used to control key squares to enable favorable trades; use it sparingly but effectively.
notes.plans: Play Kh6 to protect h6, then g5 to force queen exchange and simplify the win.

notes.explains: In a winning position with a material advantage, the two main conversion methods are opening files to infiltrate with rooks or pushing a passed pawn. Here, pushing c4 opens the b-file for the rook.
notes.teaches: When converting a winning position, focus on either activating your rook via open files or advancing a passed pawn. Practice this against a computer to improve efficiency under time pressure.
notes.plans: Push c4 to open the b-file, then infiltrate with the rook on the b-file while supporting the passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black aims to establish a light-square blockade, often with moves like h5, to control key squares such as f5 and discourage White's f5 break. This setup can lead to a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: In certain Sicilian structures, Black can voluntarily delay development (e.g., bishop on f8) to maintain a grip on critical squares like f5 and h4, then activate later.
notes.plans: Black can play Nh5 to discourage f5, or if White pushes f5 anyway, retreat to g7 to hit the pawn and prepare Rook to h4 or Queen to d7 to pressure the h-pawn.

notes.explains: Against White's Bishop d3 setup, Black can counter with e5, Bc2, and d5 to challenge the center. If White plays d3, Black can castle queenside and attack the pawn on d3.
notes.teaches: When White plays Bd3, Black can aim for an early ...d5 break to seize central space, often leading to a reversed Maroczy Bind structure.
notes.plans: After ...e5 and ...d5, if White takes on d5, recapture with the queen; if White plays d3, castle queenside and attack the d3 pawn.

notes.explains: In the line with Bb2 and Bd7, modern theory often prefers Qc2 for White to discourage d4. Black can respond with Qc7, preventing White from recapturing with a pawn after ...cxd4. If White castles, Black plays g6, and if White pushes d4 anyway, Black captures and forces White to recapture with a knight, signaling White's setup is ineffective.
notes.teaches: Black's setup aims to make it difficult for White to achieve the desirable d4 break; if White must recapture with a knight, Black has succeeded in limiting White's central control.
notes.plans: After ...g6, Black can develop with ...Nc6, ...Bg7, and expand with ...d5, as in the game Svidler-Gelfand 2014.

notes.explains: After White plays h3, Black should avoid the trap Nxe4?? (which loses a piece). Instead, Black can play g6 and allow Bg4, which gives Black an easy game. White's best response is Nbd2 to recapture on f3 with a knight, but after h3, the queen on d1 becomes awkward and White struggles to push d4.
notes.teaches: When White plays h3, Black can exploit the queen's awkward position by playing ...Bg4 and later expanding on the queenside or playing ...e5 to discourage d4.
notes.plans: After ...Nc6 and ...Bg4, Black can follow with ...Rb8, ...Nd7, and ...a5 to push the a-pawn to a3, weakening White's queenside. If White plays a4, Black can play ...Nd4, threatening tactics on b3.

notes.explains: The key is to notice the alignment of the rook on b8 and the queen on a5, which seems well defended but is vulnerable because the defenders can be forced away. The tactic works only after White has played a4, weakening the b3 square.
notes.teaches: When you see a potential fork or attack, check if the defenders are only one piece deep—if so, you may be able to force the defender away or exploit an undefended piece.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, threatening both a fork on b3 and infiltration. If White drops the queen back, play Nxb3, eliminating the dark-squared bishop and leaving White weak on dark squares. Then advance f5 to open a second front.

notes.explains: In the original position, Nd4 directly doesn't work because White can move the queen away. The correct sequence starts with Nd4, and only after White's response (like dropping the queen back) does c2 become possible, attacking both rooks.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you need to play a preparatory move (like Nd4) to create the conditions for a later tactic (like c2). The order matters—don't rush the immediate fork if it can be parried.
notes.plans: After Nd4 and White's queen retreat, play c2, attacking both rooks. White likely drops a rook, then Black evacuates the queen and wins the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: In the Najdorf Sicilian, White's bishop g5 is the most dangerous line, threatening Bxf6 to ruin Black's pawn structure. Black can defend with Nbd7 or e6, but Nbd7 is a modern resurgence.
notes.teaches: When White plays Bg5 in the Najdorf, Black must address the threat to the f6 knight. Nbd7 is a flexible defense that prepares to reroute the knight to e5.
notes.plans: Black will aim to play ...h6 to test the bishop, then ...g5 to challenge it, eventually uncoiling the position with the knight reaching e5 with tempo.

notes.explains: White's idea is to push e5, which would collapse Black's position. Black's queen on c7 coordinates pieces and prepares ...h6. The knight on d7 wants to go to e5 as an outpost.
notes.teaches: In cramped Sicilian positions, Black often uncoils by rerouting the knight to e5, gaining tempi by attacking the queen. This gambit with ...g5 is a typical way to achieve that.
notes.plans: Black will play ...h6, then ...g5 to force the bishop to g3, then push e5 to fork White's bishop and knight, winning a piece.
